rationale: A wins because it keeps the story spine tight and refuses to launder assumptions into facts. Its best angle, "Instacart's ad business hit a $1B run rate while its core delivery growth fell to single digits," has a real business tension and names the exact proof that could kill it. B has useful shapes, but lines like "a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" turn separate facts into an adoption curve the update did not give us. That is how a founder gets corrected by a reporter in sentence two.
gaps_in_A: "Caper smart carts let shoppers skip the checkout line — and they're spreading to more chains" is still product-rollout copy until a named chain or outcome shows up. A knows this, but the angle remains thin without that proof.

"Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app — what that says about retail media" needs external benchmarks before it becomes more than a scale number. A asks for comps, but the headline depends on them.
"Decay: 24hr" is overprecise for angles that are all based on disclosed company numbers. The set correctly flags "no current external news peg supplied," but does not resolve that weakness.
gaps_in_B: "With $1B in Ad Revenue" is sloppy grounding. The update says "$1B annual run rate," not trailing ad revenue.

"a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" overclaims. The update says Instacart has 1,500+ retail banners and smart carts are expanding; it does not say carts are planned across all those banners.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" imports an outside trend that was not in the update. It may be true, but this exercise is not a vibes buffet.

"With $1B in Ad Revenue and 6,000 Brands" and "What 6,000 Consumer Brands Buying Grocery Ads Reveals" are too close unless B can produce distinct buyer proof. Otherwise it is one retail-media angle wearing two jackets.
